title: Mounted pastoral nomadism on the Eurasian steppe
summary: Domestic horses spread after about 2200 BCE, but one analysis finds widespread riding began only after about 1500 BCE, though others argue for earlier riding. In the Mongolian Altai, isotope study of horses buried 3,000 years ago at Burgast reveals patterns of mobile pastoralism: herds moved seasonally.

uncertainty.note: Science Advances (Anthony et al. 2026) cites models dating widespread riding to after c. 1500 BCE; PLOS One (Zazzo et al. 2025) dates mobile horse pastoralism in western Mongolia to the Late Bronze Age (c. 1200 BCE / 3000 years ago).

as_recorded.value: widespread riding began even later, after ∼1500 BCE
beginning of the Late Bronze Age (c. 1200 BCE)
deposited within a short period of time, 3000 years ago

where.modern_name: Eurasian steppe; pin in the Mongolian Altai
where.historical_name: Mongolian Altai steppe, eastern Eurasian steppe (Late Bronze Age pastoralist territory)

importance.justification: Mounted pastoral nomadism revolutionized human mobility, continental trade, and military strategy across the Eurasian steppe, linking East Asia and Western Eurasia for millennia.

related.because: Late Bronze Age mounted pastoral nomadism provided the technological and pastoral economic foundation for the emergence of the Scythian and Saka cultures across Eurasia.
Steppe pastoral mobility opened early trans-Eurasian communication corridors that preceded the formal Silk Roads trade network.
